about: SHIP CLASSES OF 793 - every kind of craft on the water in Kapman's world, as a table the game reads (edit freely). One row per class: id; name; period_name (what it was called then, where known); cultures; waters (sea, coast, river, lake); size, heights, rig, oars, crew, cargo and speeds (units below); polar_factor (on the Gislinge ShipClass curve); uses (trade_long, coasting, fishing, ferry, river_haul, war, estate); from/to (years on the water; 0 = before the game / no end); evidence (finds and texts, short cites); look (for a placeholder: placeholder = scale factors on the Gislinge hull); uncertain (what is (?)). LATER = evidence later than 793, used only as a stand-in. Numbers are estimates from the finds and replica trials named; heights with no find behind them are scaled (method in uncertain). Sources: Viking Ship Museum (Gislinge); MASS (Utrecht 1, Graveney, Salme); Osiliana (Salme); Nordeide, Bonde & Thun 2020 (Kvalsund); Two new early mediaeval inland vessels at the Rhine (Krefeld-Gellep III); osebergvikingarv.no (Saga Oseberg); Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen (Kanhave); Annales regni Francorum; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; Bede; Willibald; Adomnan; Dicuil; Senchus fer nAlban; electronic Sawyer.

units.length_m, beam_m, draught_m, freeboard_m: metres, real world (the game applies its own scale: distances /32, heights /4)
units.freeboard_m: laden, waterline to the gunwale amidships
units.hull_top_m: waterline to the highest part of the hull (stem heads, or a cabin roof): what is seen of a boat with no mast
units.sail_top_m: waterline to the masthead; null = no mast
units.mast: true if hulls of the class carry a mast (sailing or towing); mast_share = share (0-1) of the hulls that do in 793
units.cultures, waters: ids (waters: sea, coast, river, lake); cultures_note and waters_note qualify them
units.oars: oars, both sides together (6 = 3 pairs); 0 = paddles or poles only
units.cargo_t: tonnes of cargo beyond crew and gear, typical
units.speed_sail_kn: knots through the water on a beam reach in an 8 m/s wind (the Gislinge ShipClass reference wind); null = no sail
units.speed_max_kn: knots, the most in a strong fair wind
units.speed_oars_kn: knots cruising under oars, paddles or poles in a calm
units.rowing_hours: hours the crew keeps speed_oars_kn before a rest (estimate)
units.closest_to_wind_deg: degrees off the true wind; null = cannot sail
units.polar_factor: multiplier on the Gislinge ShipClass speedByWindAngle curve: 1 = the Gislinge's polar, 0 = cannot sail; above 1 where replica trials show a faster hull; closest_to_wind_deg and speed_max_kn still apply
units.towed_upstream_km_day, downstream_km_day: km over the ground per travelling day on a river (estimates)
units.gale_fragility: 0 = rides out a gale at sea, 1 = must be ashore before it: STARTING GUESS TO TUNE
units.lookout_eye_m: metres above the water of a man standing aboard
units.placeholder: scale factors on the Gislinge hull for a 3D stand-in: length_x, beam_x, depth_x ((draught + freeboard) / 0.59 m); mast = show one by default (mast_share 0.5 or more)
units.from, to: years the class is on the water (0 = before the game / no end)

classes.name: Gislinge boat (the player's boat)
classes.period_name: batr; a six-oar boat, ON sexaeringr (?) (the Norse names are attested only later, LATER)
evidence: Viking Ship Museum, Gislinge original find: found 1993 in the reclaimed Lammefjord; tree-ring date built c. 1130; 7.7 x 1.5 m; cargo about 1 t ('four men and ten sheep'); used about 50 years, for fishing and carrying goods and people
Kapman ShipClass Gislinge_WorkingBoat.asset: freeboard 0.34 m, cargoKg 900, polar peak 5.5 kn at 130 deg, 4.8 kn on the beam, maxKnots 6.5, rowingKnots 3.5, closestToWind 58 (8 m/s reference)
crew 4: the user's decision of 2026-10-01 (Plans/ai_fleets.md)
classes.look: Slender double-ended clinker boat, low sheer, gently raised stems; 3 pairs of oars; a short mast amidships with a small square sail. The existing Gislinge model.
uncertain: LATER: built c. 1130, a stand-in for the small boats of 793 (Kvalsund I 780-800, Valsgarde, Reric, Staraya Ladoga rivets)
mast and sail reconstructed: none survived (?)
sail_top 5.0 m (?): scaled as ~0.65 of the length above the keel, like the Skuldelev 3 replica's rig; measure the Gislinge model's mast to replace it

classes.name: Scandinavian small clinker boat (faering, six-oar boat, lake and river boat)
classes.period_name: batr; ON faeringr / sexaeringr (?) (names attested later, LATER)
evidence: Kvalsund I (Sunnmore): 9.5 m rowing boat, tree-ring date 780-800 (Nordeide, Bonde & Thun 2020)
Valsgarde and Vendel boat graves (Uppland, 7th-8th c): boats of 6-15 m; two of about 10 m for 4-5 oarsmen a side
Reric (Gross Stromkendorf): 6 Scandinavian boat graves, 3 with boats of 10-15 m (rivet rows)
Staraya Ladoga: Scandinavian boat rivets from the mid-8th c; boats of 6-10 m (Archaeonautica 2022)
LATER: Gokstad faering 6.5 m (c. 900); Skuldelev 6 11.2 x 2.5 m (c. 1030); Gislinge (c. 1130)
classes.look: The Gislinge hull. Most fishing and fjord boats without a mast (mast_share).
uncertain: how many small boats carried a sail in 793 (?)

classes.name: Logboat (dugout)
classes.period_name: Latin monoxylus / linter (?); OE aesc or bat (?)
evidence: Welham Bridge (E. Yorkshire): a logboat built into a landing revetment, trackway dated AD 530-690
Langstone (Hampshire) c. AD 500; Callow (Ireland) 9th c (radiocarbon)
catalogues: McGrail 1978 (England and Wales); Mowat 1996 (154 Scottish logboats, all periods); Lanting 2000
LATER: Constantine VII, De Administrando Imperio (c. 950): Slavs cut monoxyla in winter and sell them to the Rus'
classes.look: One hollowed trunk: a long narrow trough, flat sheer, blunt ends; paddled or poled. Reads as a log with people in it.
uncertain: sizes are from all-period catalogues, not a 793 series (?)
speed is an estimate (no period figure)

classes.name: Expanded or double logboat river freighter (forerunner of the Utrecht type)
classes.cultures_note: frankish: lower Rhine, IJssel, Vecht; continental_saxon: Weser
classes.sail: towing mast; a small sail before the wind (?)
evidence: Eke (Bremen-Seehausen, Weser), 8th c: a double logboat widened with frames, 10.25 x 1.4-1.5 m (Medieval boat and ship finds of Germany, the Low Countries and NE France)
LATER: Utrecht 1 (MASS): bottom of one expanded oak trunk at least 14 m long; 17.45 x 3.84 m; capacity ca 10-15 t; small mast step near the bow suggesting towing; dendro terminus post quem 1019
classes.look: Banana-shaped: both ends sweep up from a long flat middle; no tall stems; a short mast well forward for the tow-line.
uncertain: no Utrecht-type hull securely dated to the 8th c; the Eke boat is related (?)
cargo by displacement: 10 m x 1.2 m x 0.35 m x block 0.6 = 2.5 t, minus ~0.8 t hull (?)

classes.name: Flat-bottomed plank river barge, towed upstream
classes.cultures_note: frankish: Rhineland, Ripuaria; frisian: on the Rhine; continental_saxon: Weser
classes.sail: towing mast; rarely a small sail before the wind (?)
classes.crew_range: 2-3 aboard + 3-6 hauling on the bank upstream
evidence: Krefeld-Gellep III (Rhine), 8th c (dendro): reconstructed 15.2 m; loading capacity 6,961 kg; mast step read as a towing mast (Two 'new' early mediaeval inland vessels at the Rhine)
Kalkar-Niedermormter (Rhine), c. 805: laden with building stone, at least 4.5 t
Karl (Bremen, Weser), after 808: 16-20 x 2.5-3 m
Wandalbert, Miracula S. Goaris (c. 839, LATER): a Frisian's ship hauled upstream by rope from the bank 'as is customary'
Thionville capitulary 805 (LATER): no new toll where ropes are stretched or ships pass under bridges
classes.look: Long, low and box-like; flat raked ends, no stem posts; a short sturdy towing mast a quarter of the length from the bow; cargo heaped amidships; a steering oar aft.
uncertain: Seine and Loire hulls (?): no 8th-c find
towing and drift speeds are estimates: haulers 2.5-4 km/h for ~10 h, less bends and stops; current 1-1.5 m/s for 10-12 h (?)

classes.name: River ship of a king, bishop or abbey (passengers and estate goods)
classes.period_name: Latin navis; naves of the toll charters
classes.cultures_note: frankish: royal, episcopal and monastic households; frisian: skippers hired (?)
classes.sail: towing mast; a sail before the wind now and then (?)
evidence: Annales regni Francorum 793: in autumn Charles went by boat from Regensburg to the Fossa Carolina, then by ship to the Main; RFA 792: a bridge of boats built at Regensburg
Charlemagne's charter D.122 (27 March 779) for Saint-Germain-des-Pres: its ships going up and down the rivers are free of toll
Cormery (Loire/Indre): 2 boats free of toll in 800, for grain, wine and salt (Juvenes, books.openedition.org/cidehus/19294)
Rimbert, Vita Anskarii ch. 7 (LATER, 826): Bishop Hadebald of Cologne gives 'a good boat' with two cabins, down the Rhine past Dorestad
classes.look: A barge or long river boat with a low wooden cabin or awning (hull_top_m is the cabin roof); a few well-dressed passengers; no flags or banners (none attested).
uncertain: hull type assumed from the barges and logboat freighters (?)

classes.name: Small plank skiff or punt (river ferry for people, lighter, errand boat)
evidence: Pactus legis Salicae tit. XXI 'De navibus furatis' (c. 507-511): fines for taking or stealing another man's boat
LATER: IV Aethelred 2 (c. 1000), Billingsgate: a small boat (navicula) 1/2d, a larger one with a sail 1d, a keel or hulk 4d
classes.look: Short, low and wide; square or raked ends (punt) or a pointed bow (skiff); one pair of oars, a sculling oar or a pole.

classes.name: Horse and cart ferry
classes.period_name: Latin navigium (the ferry of the capitularies) (?)
evidence: Size from the load: a cart and its oxen weigh about 1-1.5 t; or 2-3 horses; or 15-20 people (estimate)
Capitularies on tolls (Thionville 805 c. 13 and repeats, LATER but codifying custom): toll only where a bridge or ferry (navigium) is provided (?)
Einhard, Vita Karoli 17: the Mainz Rhine bridge (500 paces, ten years building) burned in 813, so before c. 803 the crossing there was by boat (?)
LATER: Walenstadt harbour with shipping and ferry tolls given to Sackingen in 965 (HLS)
classes.look: A wide flat punt, square ends, low sides; a cart, horses or cattle standing in it; poled, rowed or pulled along a rope (?).

classes.name: Timber raft
evidence: Bede, Prose Life of Cuthbert ch. 3 (c. 721): monks of the monastery at the Tyne mouth bring timber down the Tyne on rafts; a west wind carries them out to sea
classes.look: A platform of lashed logs just above the water; men with poles and steering sweeps; it drifts with the current (cargo_t = the raft itself, 5-30 t (?)).

classes.name: Gaelic currach (hide boat on a wooden frame)
classes.period_name: Latin curuca / curucus; Old Irish curach
evidence: Adomnan, Vita Columbae (c. 697-700): curucae (hide boats) beside wooden boats built on Iona

Dicuil, De mensura orbis terrae (825), of voyages c. 795: to the northern islands in two days and two nights 'plenis velis'; in 'two summer days and the night between' in a 'navicula duorum transtrorum' (two thwarts)
Gildas (mid-6th c): 'Scotti emergent certatim de curucis'
Broighter gold model (1st c BC): a mast and 9 oars a side
classes.look: Light and buoyant: high, gently curved sheer, rounded bow, no keel post; dark hide skin, no planks or rivets; a short mast forward of amidships.
uncertain: speed from Dicuil's voyage times: ~300 km in ~48 h = 3.3 kn made good; ~40 h = 4.0-4.3 kn (?)

classes.name: Gaelic and Pictish wooden ship ('seven-bencher' of the sea muster; navis longa)
classes.period_name: Old Irish secht-sess (seven-bencher); Latin navis longa / navis oneraria
evidence: Senchus fer nAlban (core 7th c (?), copy 10th c): two seven-benchers due from every twenty houses; Cenel nGabrain 560 houses, Cenel nOengusa 430, Cenel Loairn 420 = 1,410 houses = about 141 ships
Annals of Ulster 719: sea battle of Ard Nesbi within Dal Riata
Annals of Tigernach 729: 150 Pictish ships wrecked at Ros Cuissine (Troup Head (?))
St Orland's Stone, Cossans (late 8th-early 9th c): double-ended mastless boat with high ends, a rudder and 5-6 people
Adomnan, Vita Columbae: navis longa and navis oneraria
classes.look: Double-ended, high rising ends, oars along both sides: a Norse-like rowing hull with lower, plainer stems.
uncertain: length from 7 benches x ~0.9-1.0 m + 3-5 m of ends (?)
the Senchus is an assessment, not a counted fleet (?)

classes.name: English, Frisian and Frankish small working boat (inshore fishing, weirs, ferrying, lighter)
evidence: clench nails and boat timbers from Dover-Buckland, Caister-on-Sea and Castledyke, Barton-upon-Humber (7th-9th c) (England's Maritime Archaeological Research Agenda)
Blackwater estuary fish weirs, radiocarbon 7th-9th c; Collins Creek complex ~1,660 m
Bede HE IV.13 (c. 681): Wilfrid's men cast eel-nets into the sea off Sussex and take 300 fish
Barrett, Locker & Roberts 2004: marine fish rare in English sites before c. 1000 (the 'fish event horizon')
classes.look: A Gislinge hull scaled down, mostly without a mast; nets, baskets and eel traps aboard.

classes.name: Southern Baltic coastal boat (Slav boats pegged with treenails; riveted boats at Truso and Grobina)
classes.waters_note: lake: lagoons, Lake Druzno; river: mouths
evidence: Truso (Janow Pomorski), c. 750-850: remains of clinker boats with iron rivets 9-11 m long, 2.5-3 m wide; barrels of tar, split and unused rivets (repair) (Jagodzinski, abstract) (?)
LATER: Szczecin boat 8 m (early 9th c); Ralswiek 2 9.8 x 2.8 m (9th-10th c); Frombork 17 m and 6-7 m (8th-11th c (?)); Puck 2 (10th c), treenails and moss caulking
classes.look: Like a Norse boat but beamier, with lower stems; rows of wooden peg heads instead of rivet heads on Slav boats (a texture detail).
uncertain: cargo by displacement: 10 x 2.6 x 0.5 x 0.55 = ~7 m3 minus 2-3 t of hull (?)

classes.name: Norse all-purpose sailing and rowing ship, 12-18 m (trader, envoy, warband ship)
classes.period_name: ON skip (ship) (?); the knarr is LATER
evidence: Salme II (Saaremaa), c. 750: 17-17.5 x 3 m; keel outline and rivet rows indicate a sail; 34 dead (Osiliana; MASS)
Salme I: 11.5 x 2 m, probably ~6 pairs of oars, rowing; 7 dead
Kvalsund ship (Sunnmore): tree-ring date 780-800; ~18 x 3.2 m; removable side rudder; no mast step found
Reric boat graves 10-15 m; Kanhave canal (Samso, 726-729): 500 x 11 m, draughts up to ~1 m
speeds, LATER: Roar Ege (Skuldelev 3 replica) 4-5 kn average, 8-10 kn top; Wulfstan Hedeby-Truso '7 days and nights under sail' (~2.2 kn made good); Ohthere Kaupang-Hedeby in 5 days
classes.look: Long, low, double-ended clinker hull; stems 2-3 m above the water; one mast amidships with a square wool sail; side rudder on the starboard quarter; shorter and beamier than the longship, fewer oars manned.
uncertain: cargo with a full crew (?): Skuldelev 3 (14 m, LATER) carries 4-5 t with 5-8 men
sail_top 9 m (?): ~0.6 of the length above the keel

classes.name: Norse warship (the raiders' ship), 18-27 m
classes.period_name: ON langskip / skeid (names attested later, LATER); OE aesc (?)
classes.cultures_note: norse: Hordaland, Rogaland, Vestfold; danish: kings' ships
classes.rowing_sprint: 5.5 kn for 1.5 h, then 4 kn (the approved plan's chase rule; estimate)
evidence: ASC 789 (D, E, F: from Hordaland): 3 ships of Northmen at Portland; Aethelweard: the reeve Beaduheard rode from Dorchester thinking them traders
ASC 793 and Alcuin's letters of 793: Lindisfarne sacked
Storhaug, Karmoy (Avaldsnes): built c. 770, buried 779; keel ~22 m (Bill & Daly 2012); a sailing ship (Ditta) (?)
Kvalsund (780-800): ~18 m, ~10 pairs of oars
LATER: Oseberg (built 820) 21.6 x 5.1 m, 15 pairs of oar holes; Saga Oseberg replica 21.5 x 5.2 m, 28 oars, crew 40-45, rows 3-4 kn, sails 10-12 kn top, sail 82 m2 (osebergvikingarv.no)
LATER: RFA 810, 200 ships of Godfred in Frisia
classes.look: Long and low, sweeping high stems, a row of 13-16 oar ports a side, low freeboard amidships; shields along the gunwale (Hedeby coins c. 825, LATER; Gotland stones).
uncertain: Grondhaug once dated c. 780, revised 2025 to 854-867 (disputed) (?)

classes.name: Frisian, Frankish and English sea-going merchant ship
classes.period_name: Latin navis negotiatorum; OE ceol (keel) and hulc are attested later (LATER)
classes.waters_note: river: tidal reaches: Thames, Seine to Rouen, Rhine to Dorestad
evidence: Willibald, Vita Bonifatii (763-768): in 716 Boniface paid his fare at Lundenwic and came 'with favourable winds' to Dorestad; later 'the huge sails bellied in the north-west wind' to the mouth of the Cuent (Canche)
Bede HE IV.22: a Frisian buys the captive Imma in London (679)
LATER: Graveney boat (MASS): built c. 895 (dendro, revised 1983); reconstructed 13.6 m long, ~4 m wide; 6-7 t of cargo; low freeboard; Rhenish lava querns and hops
LATER: Charlemagne's ship deniers of Quentovic and Dorestad (812-814): a ship with a mast
classes.look: Beamy and deep; modest stems; few or no oar ports; one mast amidships, square sail; no shields: shorter, broader and higher than the longship.
uncertain: the 8th-c Frisian sea-going hull is unknown: keeled clinker (Crumlin-Pedersen) or a 'hulc' with rising ends (Ellmers) (?)

classes.name: Coaster, minster and estate ship (beach-landing sailing and rowing boat, 8-12 m)
classes.period_name: Latin navis (the ships of the toll charters); OE scip
classes.cultures_note: english: Kentish, Mercian and Northumbrian minsters; frankish: Loire, Seine, Flanders
classes.waters_note: sea: short crossings; river: lower reaches
evidence: S 86 (c. 733): Aethelbald of Mercia remits to Minster-in-Thanet the toll on 1 ship at London; Rochester 1 ship, Worcester 2 ships (S 88, S 98 (?))
S 29 (763/4): Eadberht II of Kent remits to Abbess Sigeburg of Minster-in-Thanet the toll on 2 ships at Fordwich and a 3rd at Fordwich and Sarre
Cormery (800): 2 toll-free boats for salt, wine and grain
North Ferriby and other Humber beach markets (7th-8th c sceattas)
LATER analogue: Skuldelev 6 (c. 1030), 11.2 x 2.5 m
classes.look: A Gislinge-type hull scaled up: double-ended, moderate stems, broad and handy; one mast; drawn up on the foreshore at the wics at low water.
uncertain: hull inferred between the Gislinge (1 t) and Graveney (6-7 t) scales (?)

classes.name: English and Frankish war, levy and (from 800) guard ship
classes.cultures_note: english: royal levies; frankish: coastguard from 800; frisian: ships requisitioned
evidence: Sutton Hoo Mound 1 (c. 625): ~27 x 4.5 m, about 40 oars (?), no mast found
RFA 789: Frisians came by ship up the Havel to join Charlemagne against the Wilzi
Bede HE II.9 (Edwin takes Anglesey and Man), IV.26 (Ecgfrith's fleet to Ireland, 684)
LATER: RFA 800, a fleet and guards on the Gallic sea coast against pirates; RFA 811, Boulogne and Ghent fleets
classes.look: Long and low, broad amidships, with rising ends less tall and curled than Oseberg's (?); no shields or banners in 793.
uncertain: no standing fleet at sea in 793 (?)
Offa's charter S 134 (792), Kentish service against pagan seamen: wording not checked (?)

later_types_not_in_table: Norse half-decked cargo ship (knarr, byrdingr): Askekarr (built c. 900-920, ~16 m), Klastad (990s, 21 m, ~13 t), Skuldelev 1 and 3 (c. 1030-1040)
Utrecht type at full size (Utrecht 1, dendro after 1019), the hulc of IV Aethelred (c. 1000) and the cog (12th c)
Slav longship (Puck 2, first half of the 10th c, 19-20 x 2.2 m)
Oseberg (820), Gokstad (c. 890-900), Graveney (c. 895), Skuldelev 2 and 5 (c. 1030-1042): used above only as LATER stand-ins
